messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Security Guard
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 48

Meera is a sixty-six-year-old woman with a steady gaze and a slight stoop, as if she is always bracing herself. She still wears her security guard uniform—navy blue, pressed, with a badge that reads “Arcadia Plaza” in small letters—even on her days off. She says it’s because the fabric is comfortable, but the truth is she feels safer in it.

The event that changed everything happened fifteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening. Meera had just finished her shift at the mall and was driving home. Her husband, Rajesh, had called to say he was walking to the corner store to buy milk. She told him to wait, that she’d pick it up on the way. He laughed and said he needed the air. By the time she pulled into their street, the ambulance was already there. Neighbors stood in clusters, hands over their mouths. Rajesh had been hit by a speeding motorcycle as he crossed the road. He survived, but his left leg was crushed, and he spent three weeks in the ICU. Meera was the first to reach him, his blood still wet on the asphalt, his eyes wide and unseeing as strangers worked on him.

In the months that followed, Meera stopped sleeping. She would lie awake in the dark, replaying the sound of the sirens, the way her breath caught when she saw the crowd. She started checking the locks on every door three times before bed. At the mall, where she has worked for twelve years, she began walking the same patrol route over and over, counting the exits in her head. Her supervisor noticed she was snapping at shoppers who seemed “too close” or “too fast.” Two months ago, a teenage boy ran past her to catch the elevator, and she grabbed his arm so hard that he cried out. She apologized, but the shaking in her hands did not stop for an hour.

Now, in the therapy room, Meera sits upright on the edge of the chair. She talks in a low, measured voice about how she cannot let Rajesh go anywhere alone. She drives him to his physiotherapy appointments even though he says he can take the bus. She hovers when he uses the stairs. At night, she wakes from dreams where she is running toward him but the street keeps stretching longer. She does not tell him about the dreams. She does not tell him that she sometimes smells his blood in the car, even after she has cleaned it twice.

At work, Meera has become hypervigilant. She scans every parking lot for speeding vehicles. She avoids the loading dock where delivery trucks back in too fast. She argues with the other guards about break schedules, insisting on shorter rotations so she can do more walkthroughs. She knows her colleagues think she is difficult, but she cannot stop. If she lets her guard down, she is certain something terrible will happen.

Her PCL-5 score of 48 reflects the intrusion, avoidance, and negative beliefs that now rule her days. She believes she should have prevented Rajesh’s accident—if only she had answered his call sooner, if only she had driven faster. The guilt sits in her chest like a stone. She does not laugh as often as she used to. She has stopped calling her sister in Mumbai because she does not want to explain why she sounds tired.

Yet Meera keeps coming to work. She keeps waking up at 4 a.m. to make Rajesh’s tea and lay out his medications. She keeps the uniform clean. She says she does not know who she is without it. When the clinic asks if she has considered retiring, she shakes her head. “Then what would I do?” she asks, her voice flat. “Just wait?”
